title: Too many good results
hookLine: meditation trials report more positive results than expected by chance (Coronado-Montoya et al., 2016)
last: TRUST WHAT MANY STUDIES AGREE ON.

lines: A CAREFUL TRIAL, A FLAT RESULT.
cards: There's a drawer in this story. A researcher runs a careful trial of a meditation program: months of work. The result comes back flat, no clear difference between the people who meditated and the people who didn't.
It's honest, it's dull, and it's hard to get anyone excited about printing it. So the paper goes into a drawer, and the researcher moves on. Nobody lied.
Nobody cheated. Now multiply that drawer across a whole field. What reaches the public is the pile of studies that worked, and the pile looks wonderful.

teach.h: HOW MANY SHOULD COME OUT POSITIVE?
teach.b: First, the question. A team led by Stephanie Coronado-Montoya looked at published trials of mindfulness-based therapies and asked something clever. Not, does it work?

But: given how big these studies were, how many should come out positive, even if mindfulness really helps? Small studies miss real effects fairly often, so a healthy record should include some misses. Second, the answer.
The published trials reported positive results far more often than their size would predict. Too many good results: the fingerprint of missing studies. Third, where the missing ones went.
The team also checked trial registries, public lists where researchers announce a study before running it. A good share of registered trials had not been published long after they finished.
The drawer is real. Fourth, what this does and doesn't mean. It doesn't mean meditation does nothing; yesterday's review still found modest benefits.
It means the published picture is probably rosier than the full one, and the honest size of the effect is likely smaller than the brightest papers suggest.
Paul, writing to the church at Thessalonica, put the posture plainly, in the King James text: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Test first, then hold on.
Not a cynic, who throws everything out, and not a fan, who keeps everything. Someone in the middle, with a question ready.

how: Researchers check for missing studies by comparing published trials with public trial registries and with how many positive results the studies' size would predict; researchers can also announce trials in public registries before running them.

games.q: what does “too many good results” mean?
o: published trials coming out positive far more often than their size predicts
proof that mindfulness therapy works for nearly everyone who tries it
a study whose results were faked to look better than they were

games.q: too many good results: tap the pairs.
p: a public list of studies before they run

games.q: you've run a careful meditation trial, and the result is flat. what do you do?
o: put it in a drawer and move on.
publish it anyway, flat result and all.
keep reanalyzing until something looks positive.
games.why: publishing the flat result is what keeps the record honest. the drawer is what the team's counting suggests often happens instead.

practice: Think of one thing this path, or any app, book or teacher, has told you practice will do for you: calmer, kinder, sharper.

Hold it lightly, the way you'd hold a bird, and ask two things: what would it look like if this weren't true for me, and what have I actually noticed? Let both answers be allowed, and keep sitting either way.

wordCard.voice: Too many good results. When nearly every published trial is positive, some of the flat ones are probably in a drawer. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a little sceptical. A good question is its own kind of respect. That's today, done.
